titleStmt.title: Making Marx More Readable: A Minimal Computing Approach to a Community-Driven Edition of Capital Vol. 1

dhq:bio.p: Avery Wiscomb is Assistant Professor of English and Digital Humanities at Virginia Tech. His research examines how computational methods reshape knowledge production in the humanities, with a focus on the institutional politics of digital scholarship and the history of computing and AI.

dhq:authorInfo.dhq:affiliation: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

dhq:bio.p: Steven Gotzler is a Teaching Assistant Professor of English and Comparative Literature and the Associate Director of the Digital Literacy and Communications Lab at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. His research explores historical regimes of labor and work, cultural studies of games and play, and materialist theories of media and technology.

dhq:abstract.p: The following article presents MARXdown, a minimal digital reading edition of Karl Marx’s Capital Vol. 1, as a retrospective case study in applying minimal computing principles to create accessible, community-driven digital humanities (DH) projects. Developed by graduate students at Carnegie Mellon University in 2019–20, MARXdown demonstrates how framing minimal computing as practical commitments can lower access barriers, demystify computing labor, and facilitate knowledge sharing. The project leveraged lightweight, open-source tools to create a collaborative reading environment that addressed specific community needs. This approach allowed for adaptability during the COVID-19 pandemic, transforming MARXdown into a vital support for collaboratively reading Marx under lockdown. The article argues that practical commitments to minimal computing can promote replicable models for building digital reading editions, useful for distributing marginalized or banned texts in underserved communities. By unpacking some of MARXdown's development process, this study offers insights into both the potential and limitations of minimal computing in academic and community-driven contexts, contributing to discussions about accessibility, sustainability, and ethics in DH.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: How can digital tools enable collaborative reading and knowledge sharing for underserved communities with limited resources ? This article presents a case study of MARXdown, a minimal digital reading edition of Karl Marx's Capital Vol. 1 (1867) originally developed for graduate students at Carnegie Mellon University .

MARXdown aimed to increase access to Capital Vol. 1, enabling community annotations, and relevant commentary using accessible tools for collectively implementing a minimal reading edition online. As Roopika Risam argues, such collaborative, locally situated digital approaches can help address equity gaps and reshape the digital cultural record in academia, even with limited resources .

MARXdown's development demonstrates how minimal computing can be approached as practical commitments. By practical commitments, we refer to the concrete, actionable decisions and trade-offs made by digital humanists when applying minimal computing principles in the context of their work. Practical commitments represent the situated choices practitioners make when confronting real constraints of resources, expertise, time, and community needs. Being intentional about what these commitments are, and how we cultivate them, ensures that minimal computing principles remain rooted in embodied practice, rather than ossifying into a set of purely abstract ideals. Therefore, practical commitments emerge directly from an ongoing process that lies at the core of minimal computing: the ongoing negotiation between what is desirable and what is feasible. Throughout what follows, we use this term to emphasize how MARXdown's development involved continuous decision-making about what to prioritize, what to simplify, and what to forgo entirely—not as compromises but as affirmative choices that aligned our project with both minimal computing principles and our community's specific requirements.

These commitments reorient DH practices towards accessibility, transparency, and collaborative knowledge sharing. We argue that MARXdown, despite its obvious limitations, offers a replicable model for minimal digital reading editions. This model is valuable for sharing marginalized texts, orphan and public-domain works, or banned books in underserved communities.

MARXdown emerged from specific community needs we experienced as graduate students. Our reading group faced practical challenges: fluctuating membership as students entered and left the program, limited financial resources for purchasing multiple copies of texts, difficulties in maintaining a cohesive record of our collective engagement with Marx, and the need to reconcile different editions and translations. These constraints demanded a solution that would enable persistent yet flexible collaborative reading across changing circumstances.

As we'll discuss, these situated needs shaped our approach to minimal computing. Rather than aiming to create a comprehensive scholarly resource, we prioritized accessibility, collaborative annotation, and communal knowledge-building—essential functions for any reading community.

div.head: Background and related work
div.p: We first presented MARXdown as a generalizable model at the 2019 Cultural Studies Association (CSA) conference . A 90-minute workshop demonstrated using Jekyll for deploying static websites and the Ed. Jekyll template to create collaborative reading editions.

Comparing MARXdown to variorum editions like the Frankenstein Variorum and light-weight scholarly editions such as Walter Benjamin Digital or Electronic Beowulf, highlighted the unique community participation enabled by minimal reading editions versus complex variorum or labor-intensive scholarly editions. Feedback from presentations at other conferences such as at the Association of Computers and the Humanities and the Modern Language Association encouraged further development of the minimal computing model for digital reading editions we outline below.

Walter Benjamin Digital offers a particularly instructive comparison to MARXdown, as both projects engage with foundational theoretical texts using minimal computing principles, though with different emphases. Where Walter Benjamin Digital uses TEI-Light for encoding while maintaining a visually minimal interface, MARXdown prioritized Markdown for its lower technical barrier to entry. Both projects negotiate similar tensions between scholarly rigor and accessibility. Walter Benjamin Digital incorporates facsimile images alongside transcriptions, creating a richer documentary resource, while MARXdown focused on enhancing readability of, and collaborative engagement with, the text itself.

Our presentations at conferences revealed significant interest in minimal computing approaches that could address common challenges in graduate education and reading groups. Attendees consistently noted difficulties similar to what our group experienced: maintaining continuity amid changing membership, preserving collective knowledge, and creating accessible reading environments for texts that are often challenging both intellectually and materially to engage with. These conversations reinforced our understanding that MARXdown's design decisions—which prioritized reader experience over scholarly comprehensiveness—responded to widespread needs in academic communities.

The practical constraints that shaped MARXdown align closely with the core values of minimal computing. When faced with limited resources and specific community requirements, we found that minimal computing offered not just technical solutions but a framework for thinking about digital project development that centered accessibility and sustainability over feature richness. These considerations led us to conceptualize what we call a digital reading edition—distinct from more comprehensive scholarly editions—as will be explored in subsequent sections.

In sum, we found throughout our discussions with attendees that minimal computing principles, especially when framed as practical commitments, could help lower access barriers, facilitate knowledge sharing, and prioritize reader empowerment over back-end complexity. When put into practice, practical commitments to minimal computing can promote adaptable models for building digital reading editions that enable situated communities to engage with texts relevant to their shared contexts.
